newsitem.title: GERMANY: Meister-not certain Bonn to hit EMU deficit goal.
newsitem.headline: Meister-not certain Bonn to hit EMU deficit goal.

text.p: Bundesbank board member Edgar Meister said on Friday it was still not certain that Bonn would hit the budget deficit goal for entry to a single European currency and also called for a small starting group.

In a speech in Frankfurt to commemorate the 75-year anniversary of the establishment of the Badische Beamtenbank, Meister said, "Many countries are finding difficulties in bringing their annual deficits under the level of three percent laid down in the Maastricht Treaty.
"There is still not sufficient certainty that Germany will actually succeed," he added, according to a text of the speech.

Stressing that the 1998 decision on who makes the grade for EMU must be taken on the basis of whether long-term stability had been achieved, Meister attacked attempts by some countries to use creative accounting methods to hit the deficit target.
"Accounting tricks, which push a part of the deficit forward, as well as unrepeatable one-off effects would not be a good basis for a decision on monetary union," he said.
The decision should be taken primarily on the basis of 1997 data, but with some heed paid to past data and future plans.

"Ultimately the order of the day must be that convergence is more important than deadlines and actually achieved convergence results from the 1997 year are more important than forecasts for 1998," Meister said.
The need for a stable monetary union, which would create a satisfactory follow-up currency for the mark, meant that a high level of long-term convergence was needed.
"This would also imply a homogeneous, if smaller, group of participants in the third stage of monetary union," he said.

Noting the tendency in financial markets for convergence trading on speculation as to whether a country would enter EMU in 1999, Meister said that while markets would play a role in the final assessment, they would not dictate the decision.

"Although the feed-back from the markets should undoubtedly also be taken carefully into account by the politicians, the political decision on the participation of individual countries in monetary union cannot be left to the markets," Meister said.
"Whether the behaviour of financial markets will be confirmed in every instance by the politicial decisions which have yet to be reached remains to be seen," he added.
"In this context it can therefore not be excluded that sentiment will intermittently run hot and cold."
